extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, Judge Advocate General's office, War Department officials, and attorneys handling military records and pardons
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards concerning the custody, amendment, disclosure, destruction of War Department official records, and the principles, limits, and practice governing executive pardons in military law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of War Department official papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Official papers on file in the War Department are not public records open to inspection by any citizen; they are confidential archives consultable or for which copies may be furnished only by authority of the Secretary of War, except where law or usage provides for furnishing or courts properly require their exhibition in evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War will consider nature of information sought and proposed use to determine whether private interests outweigh public considerations. Distinguish permanent records (general/special orders, muster rolls, discharges, commissions) from reports/communications of officers, the latter generally privileged and not producible in evidence on public policy grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of records furnished only on limited bases
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department's established practice is to decline to furnish copies of records except on a call from Congress or one of its committees, upon order of a United States court, or upon request from another executive branch office for official use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical recipients when copies are furnished include accounting officers of the Treasury, the Land Office, the Indian Bureau, etc. Requests by private individuals (even Members of Congress seeking copies to prepare legislation) may be refused depending on discretion and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate required for copies to aid administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Where copies of War Department bonds, papers, or records are necessary to aid in administration of justice, it is usual to require a certificate from the tribunal stating that the documents are necessary and material to the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice helps limit disclosure of confidential departmental records to situations where judicial necessity is established; see cited practice C.19264 (July–Sept. 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: No official may alter official records of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: No War Department official or other executive officer is empowered to so change a record of fact as to make it state a fact which is not a fact; only Congress can grant relief that would effectively alter such facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records may be amended only to correct erroneous entries to make them state the truth (by the person who made them or by duly authorized entry). Statutory requirements for amendment are exceptions and must be strictly observed and confined to cases within the statute's purview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges and specifications are public documents and must be preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges and specifications referred to a court-martial for trial are public documents and there is no authority for their destruction; after arraignment they should be returned to the judge advocate who filed them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After trial, statements of service in desertion convictions should be forwarded to the Judge Advocate General; in other cases returned to department headquarters for filing in the judge advocate's office (C.15833, Jan. 28, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction of useless official papers permitted by Secretary of War
rubrics_metrics.description: Useless and valueless official papers pertaining to records of military headquarters, posts, or stations may lawfully be destroyed by order of the Secretary of War without resort to legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority is limited to papers properly classified as valueless and pertains to executive departments in Washington and related records (P.63, Jan. 1894; J.16319, May 12, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticated departmental copies admissible as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of books, records, papers, or documents in executive departments, authenticated under the seals of such departments respectively, shall be admitted in evidence equally with the originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory authorization (sec. 882, R.S.) means certified departmental copies can be used in courts in place of originals, subject to the usual rules of authentication.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's pardoning power is complete and exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Article II, section 2 of the Constitution confers complete pardoning power on the President; Congress may not control, add to, or detract from this power nor vest it in subordinate officers such as the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts by Congress to authorize the Secretary of War to revoke or set aside court-martial proceedings were held beyond constitutional power. Pardoning power cannot be extended to reach executed sentences that the President himself cannot remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardon must be delivered and accepted; revocable until delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: A pardon, like a deed, must be delivered to and accepted by the party to whom it is granted; it may be revoked before delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no pardon of a deceased person even if heirs would benefit. Example: a pardon issued but not delivered because the prisoner escaped by a forged instrument was revoked; pardons are presumed accepted on actual or constructive notice in absence of express rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full pardon removes all unexecuted penal consequences and disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A full pardon relieves the party from all punishment remaining to be suffered and removes disqualifications attached by United States statute or Army regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the unexecuted portion of imprisonment is remitted, additional penalties contingent on future events (e.g., dishonorable discharge scheduled at end of term) cannot be enforced after the pardon; the pardoned person is relieved from all future penal consequences from the date the pardon takes effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power extends to continuing punishments (loss of files, reduction in rank)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pardoning power reaches continuing punishments (such as loss of files or reduction in relative rank) and may restore an officer to former rank according to commission date, though lost promotion opportunities accrued in the meantime are not restored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoration of rank may be ordered but promotion opportunities lost during the intervening period remain forfeited; these are treated as continuing punishments remediable by pardon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential pardon can restore citizenship forfeited by desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal presidential pardon has been treated in practice as restoring citizenship forfeited by desertion; a mere remission by a court-martial does not have this effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple holdings and practice citations support that only a formal Executive pardon restores the rights of citizenship lost by desertion (C.3010, June 1897; C.11345, Oct. 1901; C.16215, Apr. 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for recommending pardon (mitigating circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judge Advocate General has recommended pardons or remissions on grounds including: minor at enlistment; enlistment under false representations by recruiter; enlisted as a raw recruit without Articles read; imperfect English comprehension; being an Indian scout unfamiliar with language or Articles; offense induced by harsh or injudicious treatment by superior; excessive or unreasonable duty; provocation; confinement impairing health; unreasonable delay between arrest/trial/approval; voluntary return after desertion; previous good character; good conduct under sentence; faithful prior service; prompt surrender; service in disaster relief; insanity since before charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grounds may be considered alone or in combination; in officers' cases, principal favorable grounds include prior good service/efficiency, high personal character, and absence of fraudulent or criminal intent. Recommendations often cite multiple favorable circumstances and prior records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition precedent for pardoning embezzlers or thieves
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases involving larceny of public property, conversion of public funds, or escapes while under charge for such offenses, a pardon should generally be conditioned upon making good the funds appropriated or restoring property or its value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical advisory practice recommends requiring restitution as a condition precedent for pardon in such fiscal or property offenses (R.1, Oct. 1862; later citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not entertain pardon applications from fugitives until surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications from deserters at large or officers/soldiers who have escaped custody should generally not be entertained until the fugitive returns and surrenders to military authorities to stand trial or abide by sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This has been the consistent advice of the Judge Advocate General over many years and across numerous cited opinions and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardon is not retroactive and cannot erase past facts of guilt
rubrics_metrics.description: A pardon is not retroactive; it cannot remit an executed punishment or restore an executed forfeiture, cannot alter past history, reverse completed records, or erase the fact that the recipient was guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pardon operates from the time it takes effect; it does not annihilate prior guilty facts and proceeds on the theory the party was guilty. It cannot remove a prior charge from the record where the offender had become a civilian and the record is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardon cannot reach fully executed sentences or restore fines paid into Treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: A pardon cannot reach or remit a fully executed sentence (e.g., corporal punishment fully inflicted) nor restore an officer or soldier legally separated by an approved dismissal or a dishonorable discharge; nor can it restore fines paid or forfeited when the amounts have been paid into the U.S. Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, where money or punishment remains unexecuted or remains in the hands of a disbursing officer, the unexecuted portion may be remitted; Congress alone can restore pay fully forfeited and pecuniarily indemnify an officer/soldier for consequences of a legally executed sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardon of political offense does not preclude trial for non-political crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: A party pardoned for a political offense, or who accepted amnesty, is not thereby relieved from amenability to trial and punishment for crimes not of a political character committed by him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic amnesties (e.g., 1865, 1868 proclamations) exemplify the principle that political pardon does not immunize against unrelated criminal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial practice for wartime deserters who fled abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of policy in certain historical contexts (e.g., Civil War deserters who fled to Canada and remained until the war's end), applications for pardon by such persons were advised to be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects a discretionary policy judgement grounded in the gravity of shirking a grave public duty in time of national peril and longstanding advisory precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of summary discharge while serving sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier summarily discharged while confined under sentence may be discharged from service and such summary discharge effects a remission of the portion of the sentence that remained unexecuted on the date of discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited holdings show summary discharge while serving sentence remits unexecuted portion (P.53, May 1892; multiple cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Full pardon does not automatically restore reenlistment eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A full pardon of a deserter does not render him eligible for reenlistment if his prior term of service was not honest and faithful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous cited decisions hold that pardon does not erase the character of prior service where it disqualifies for reenlistment (multiple citations: C.1883; C.1765; C.3125; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive pardon: actions that do or do not constitute it
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain administrative acts may or may not amount to a constructive pardon: withdrawal of a pending charge upon a pledge to abstain is not a pardon; reappointment of a dismissed officer does not condone the dismissal; promotion while awaiting trial does not constitute constructive pardon; promotion while serving sentence may be a constructive pardon if inconsistent with further operation of the sentence; promotion by selection outside regular promotion lines may be constructive pardon; promotion by seniority alone is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an act constitutes a constructive pardon depends on consistency with the sentence's further operation and on the manner of advancement (selection vs seniority). Specific citations (C.14389, C.25574, P.47) provide case examples and distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remission (definitions and effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remission is the release from punishment; it may be irrevocable; remission can result in crediting a sentence with time previously served; discharge of a soldier while serving sentence has specific remission effects; in cases of double sentence remission of the unexecuted portion of one does not affect the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pardoning power may remit portions of sentences at different times; remission rules govern credit for time served and interaction of multiple sentences (citations: 8 Op. Atty. Gen. and multiple departmental decisions).
